newsitem.title: USA: Compuserve upgrades, starts move to web.
newsitem.headline: Compuserve upgrades, starts move to web.

text.p: It's safe to say CompuServe Corp. has had a bad year.

Membership at the country's oldest major commercial online service has stagnated at 2.5 million in the United States and Canada and 5.2 million worldwide, while archrival America Online Inc. has passed the 6 million mark.
Analysts say the Columbus, Ohio, company is cutting jobs after reporting a $29.6 million loss for the 90 days that ended July 31 and is anticipating another loss this quarter.

Last week, the industry trade magazine Interactive Week quoted sources close to the company as saying CompuServe recently slashed $100 million from its marketing budget. CompuServe officials said the report was a rumour and won't comment.

CompuServe parent H&R Block Inc. spun off 15 percent of the online service in a February public stock offering but called off a subsequent sale of the remaining shares after the stock dipped to under $11 from a high of $35.50.
On Wednesday, CompuServe dropped 37.5 cents to $13.125 in afternoon trading on Nasdaq.
Amid the black clouds, CompuServe Monday tried to shed a few rays of light by unveiling the first major upgrade of its user software in almost a year.
At the same time, CompuServe revealed more of its plans to eventually move the service to the Internet, an initiative the company has dubbed "Red Dog."

It's a direction that's also luring competitors Prodigy and Microsoft Network, both of which are in the middle of transforming their once-proprietary private networks into Internet services. Microsoft Corp. is expected to unveil a revamped MSN on Oct. 10.

With CompuServe's software upgrade, subscribers to the online network launched way back in 1979 can for the first time dial into the service without having to go through the company's telecommunications network.
What does that mean? If a customer would rather dial into CompuServe, using an account with an Internet service provider such as Netcom or Mindspring, they can.

For now, subscribers will continue to pay CompuServe's $9.95 monthly fee and additional usage charges no matter how they log on. Eventually, however, CompuServe will establish separate, discounted fees for subscribers who don't log on through the company's network.
Cathy Gerber, a CompuServe member marketing manager, wouldn't say when those discounts might be announced.

However, the first CompuServe subscribers to take advantage of the service's unbundled network access and content could very well come from AT&T Worldnet, the telecommunication giant's consumer Internet service.
CompuServe expects to announce discounts by the end of the year for subscribers who log on through AT&T Worldnet. America Online and AT&T have a similar deal.
Such arrangements show CompuServe could be headed in the right direction, said Alan Weiner, an Internet analyst with Dataquest.

"It puts the emphasis on what's important in that business, the quality of the information," Weiner said. "Given the vision most people have of CompuServe as being chock full of business information, the (company) would want to make it as accessible to as many people as possible, which means putting it on the Web."
But there is a downside to moving content to the Web, according to Weiner.
"The quality of their content has never been on the measuring block before," he said. "If no one comes, that could be embarrassing," he said.
CompuServe's new user software comes in two flavors, version 2.5 for users of Windows 3.1, and version 3.0, for people using the more powerful, 32-bit Windows 95 or NT operating systems.
Version 3.0 features closer links between information on the online service and the Web.

It lets people do more than one thing at a time while online -- download a file and visit a chat room for example -- and has a "To Do" feature that lets users create a list of tasks such as sending e-mail or retrieving files that will be performed automatically at the end of a session.
The software comes with Microsoft Internet Explorer 3.0 as the default Web browser, the fruit of an agreement forged between CompuServe and Microsoft earlier this year.

Updates in version 2.5 are not as dramatic. Internet Explorer 2.1 replaces Spry Mosaic as the Web browser and graphics for the service's front door and gateways to major departments have been improved.
In both versions, improvements to technical software will make the service run faster, said marketing manager Gerber.

CompuServe is mailing a CD-ROM with copies of both versions of the new software to all current subscribers. Others can order the software by calling (800) 848-8199. A Macintosh version is due later this fall.
